# Education in Poland
Poland’s education system comprises eight years of compulsory primary school beginning at age six or seven, followed by various forms of upper secondary education. A major reform in 2017 abolished the previous two-tier system of six years primary plus three years of gimnazjum (junior high school), extending primary schooling to eight years. Upon completion, students can pursue general upper secondary (liceum) leading to the "Matura" exam for university entry, or technical and vocational schools, which also offer pathways to tertiary education. Mentally or physically handicapped students have access to special schools to prepare for the Matura.
Tertiary education follows the Bologna process, typically with three-year bachelor programs and two-year master's programs, though some fields offer single extended master’s studies (e.g. medicine). University grading uses a numeric scale from 2.0 (fail) to 5.0 (excellent), with intermediate steps. Foreign language instruction is emphasized, with most students learning one or two languages alongside Polish. The country has a long tradition of education, with institutions such as Jagiellonian University established in 1364, and compulsory education introduced nationwide in 1919. Poland's education reforms since 1999 have notably improved its international rankings in reading, science, and mathematics. Notable recent reforms have further shaped curriculum content and school structures.
